results.title: AWS Raises the Price Tag on AI Boom; Pay 20% for GPU Instances from July 1
highlights:
Amazon has made a point to investors in the AI boom that every query and inference comes with a real price tag, which Wall Street better take note of. Last week, the company quietly raised prices by a whopping 20% on some of the most sought-after AI hardware in the cloud market such as Nvidia Blackwell, H100 and H200 systems.

> Amazon Web Services (AWS) posted an update on its blog on the pricing for Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML – a reservation product that allows customers to lock in accelerator capacity for machine learning workloads. What’s interesting in the announcement is that it does not represent a broad price hike for every AWS product or solution.

...

“Effective July 1, 2026, hourly rates per accelerator will be: P6-B300 at $14.04 (all available AWS Regions except AWS GovCloud Regions), P6-B200 at $12.355 (all available Regions except AWS GovCloud Regions), P5 at $5.191 (all available US Regions), P5 at $4.72 (all available non-US Regions), P5e at $5.97 (all available Regions), P5en at $6.865 (all available US Regions), P5en at $6.241 (all available non-US Regions), and P4de at $2.214 (all available US Regions). All other prices remain unchanged,” the blog says.

...

Readers would be aware that Capacity Blocks for ML is an AWS product that allows enterprises to secure GPU instances for a future date to handle time-bound workloads such as LLM training or retraining. Customers pay a premium over spot-market rates to guarantee availability and AWS has jacked up the premium by around 20%.

...

However, AWS has highlighted that the latest price changes only apply to one purchasing option, noting that cloud customers can pick other AI workloads for which prices would remain unchanged. For how long? Well, that’s for the customers to risk on.

results.title: AWS hikes specialised AI GPU prices by 20% amid supply constraints | Noah Intelligence
highlights:
Amazon Web Services is raising prices on some of its most specialised AI computing capacity by about 20% from 1 July, according to AWS and reporting by industry outlets. The increase applies to EC2 Capacity Blocks for machine learning, a reservation product used by enterprises that need to lock in access to scarce, high-end Nvidia GPUs for training and fine-tuning models. Standard EC2 instances are not affected.

...

The updated pricing covers AWS’s highest-end accelerator families, including systems built on Nvidia’s Blackwell, Hopper and A100 hardware. New hourly rates per accelerator include $14.040 for P6-B300, $12.355 for P6-B200, $6.865 for P5en in the US, $5.970 for P5e, $5.191 for P5 in US regions and $2.214 for P4de in the US, according to AWS and market reports. AWS said these reservation prices are adjusted periodically in line with supply and demand.

results.title: The neocloud gold rush is over. The consolidation is brutal. | Meysam M.
highlights:
In 2023-2024, over 60 GPU cloud startups raised money betting they could build the next AWS for AI. Most won't survive 2026.

Here's what's separating winners from losers:
→ Winners locked in long-term contracts at $1.8-2.2/hr when H100s were scarce
→ Losers signed spot-market deals that evaporated when Blackwell supply came online
→ Winners built proprietary networking fabric (400Gbps+ InfiniBand clusters)
→ Losers resold commodity hardware with zero differentiation
The problem: hyperscalers aren't sleeping. AWS, Google, and Azure now offer H200 and GB200 capacity at prices neoclouds can't match without losing money.

Three neoclouds will survive at scale. The rest become acquisition targets or shut down.

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Rise (July 1, 2026): What It Means for AI GPU Costs | Windows Forum
highlights:
A mazon Web Services will raise prices on selected EC2 Capacity Blocks for machine learning on July 1, 2026, affecting high-end GPU reservations used for AI training, simulation, rendering, and other accelerated workloads across multiple AWS regions. The move is narrow in product scope but broad in meaning: the cloud’s old assumption that compute gets cheaper over time is being stress-tested by the economics of AI hardware. For enterprises, startups, and research teams, the price change is a reminder that the scarce resource is no longer just “cloud capacity.” It is memory-rich, networked, schedulable GPU capacity at the exact moment everyone else wants it too.

The AWS price update is not a general-purpose EC2 increase, and that distinction matters. It applies to EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, a reservation model designed for customers that need guaranteed access to clusters of accelerated instances during a defined window. In plainer terms: if you need a pile of NVIDIA GPUs for a training run, a simulation campaign, or a rendering job, AWS lets you reserve that capacity ahead of time rather than gamble on availability when the job is ready. That product exists because AI infrastructure is not fungible in the way a midrange virtual machine is fungible. A web server can often move from one family, zone, or region with modest pain. A distributed training job built around H100, H200, B200, or B300-class accelerators is another matter entirely; the job wants a large pool of identical hardware, fast interconnects, enough memory, and a scheduler that does not turn a planned run into an archaeological dig through failed provisioning attempts. The economics behind the update are also unusually transparent by cloud standards. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page now lists rates effective July 1, 2026, including per-accelerator hourly rates for P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de capacity. The figures vary by instance class and region, but the direction is unmistakable: the premium end of GPU cloud is being repriced around constrained supply rather than around the historical cloud narrative of steady commoditization. That is what makes this more than a procurement footnote. AWS is not merely adjusting a SKU buried in a pricing table. It is putting a market signal directly in front of customers who have treated hyperscale GPU capacity as the elastic substrate beneath their AI roadmaps.

results.title: L4 Up 119.2% in GPU Rental Market — Week of June 22 - June 28, 2026 | AIMC | AIMC
highlights:
The NVIDIA L4 posted the largest single-SKU median price move tracked by Ai Mining Co. this week, rising 119.2% from $0.39 to $0.86 per GPU-hour across reporting marketplaces. That movement stands in sharp contrast to last week's relatively compressed dispersion, where no individual SKU exceeded double-digit percentage shifts in either direction. For the period June 22–28, AIMC collected 6,170 observations across 31 marketplaces and 110 distinct GPU SKUs. Beyond the L4, upward pressure was broad but uneven: the A100 PCIe 80GB gained 27.9%, reaching $1.79 per GPU-hour, and the H100 PCIe advanced 19.2% to $2.73, while the B200 SXM held flat at $5.89 across 11 marketplaces. The data this week segments naturally by tier — consumer-grade, professional mid-range, and datacenter-class — and each tells a different story.
